source.title: Normalization and effective learning rates in reinforcement learning
source.authors: Clare Lyle; Ze-Yu Zheng; Khimya Khetarpal; James Martens; H. V. Hasselt; Razvan Pascanu; Will Dabney

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no apparent truncation or corruption.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports experiments on how normalization and parameter-norm projection affect training dynamics and performance, bearing conceptually on V6’s normalization claim. It does not test the claimed batch-normalization speed or higher learning-rate tolerance.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results involving CIFAR-10 classification and learning, but these do not test training classification error from random initialization as V1 states. Initialization, depth-without-shortcuts, width, and above-stability learning-rate claims are discussed or cited, not tested here. The NaP comparisons that report final benchmark accuracy test a different intervention and are not results on V6’s batch-normalization intervention.
record.test_reason: The study measures plasticity, effective learning-rate dynamics, NaP performance, and LayerNorm/RMSNorm effects. None directly tests V1–V6. In particular, LayerNorm comparisons do not test batch normalization, and stationary image-classification test accuracy does not establish near-zero training error. The record's tests/T2 classification and V6 tested_not_extracted status should be corrected.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that constraining activation and parameter norms mitigates plasticity loss and makes effective learning-rate schedules explicit. Constant effective learning rates can hurt Rainbow performance; suitable explicit decay schedules allow NaP to improve performance and robustness to nonstationarity.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates LayerNorm and its Normalize-and-Project (NaP) protocol, including parameter projection and learning-rate schedules. It does not reproduce the batch-normalization experiments described by V6.
record.method_sensitivity: In Rainbow agents, constant effective learning rate with NaP often underperforms unconstrained parameters; adding a linear learning-rate schedule improves performance. In continual random-label learning, outcomes vary by architecture and plasticity-preserving method. These findings do not establish V6’s batch-normalization speed or learning-rate-tolerance claim.

fits_no_version.finding: Figures 1 and 4 show that constraining parameter norms alongside LayerNorm improves retained learning performance during repeated random-label CIFAR-10 training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Controlling activation and parameter norms can mitigate plasticity loss in continual classification.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 2 shows that per-layer learning-rate rescaling reproduces an unconstrained normalized network's dynamics; global rescaling approximates them.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Explicit learning-rate schedules can reproduce implicit schedules caused by parameter-norm growth in scale-invariant networks.

fits_no_version.finding: Tables 1–2 report comparable stationary image-classification test accuracy for NaP and baseline models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: NaP preserves final test accuracy on the tested CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-1k benchmarks.

fits_no_version.finding: Figures 3 and 6 show that constant effective learning rates can impair Rainbow performance, while explicit decay improves performance in several games.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Effective learning-rate decay can be important for value-based deep RL performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 5 shows improved sequential Atari learning with NaP, including second-visit progress comparable to fresh initialization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: NaP improves robustness to sequential task changes in the tested Rainbow agents.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix C.3 reports that normalization and weight projection accelerate retrieval and memorization learning in small transformers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Layer normalization and weight projection can accelerate learning in the tested sequence tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: Proposition 1 and Appendix C.4 show that pre-activation normalization permits gradients through saturated units and facilitates their recovery with adaptive updates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pre-activation RMSNorm or LayerNorm can help saturated ReLU units recover under adaptive optimization.

record.problems: The CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-1k benchmark results are test accuracies, not training classification errors. Several relevant comparisons are presented only in figures in the supplied text, without numeric values. The paper does not test the exact batch-normalization claim in V6.
record.rows_left_out: No rows meet the version-specific row criteria: the paper’s reported results do not test the behavior named by V1–V5 or V6. The NaP benchmark accuracies concern a different intervention than V6’s batch-normalization comparison; the CIFAR-10 continual-learning findings concern plasticity and effective learning rates rather than whether networks fit training labels to near-zero error.

untested.parts: Near-zero training classification error in sufficiently large CNNs on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, including random labels, and its dependence on size, stopping, and regularization. Appendix B.4 says the networks could solve single tasks but provides no corresponding training-error result.
Spurious local minima in two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems and their reduction with extra student neurons.
Depth-dependent training degradation in plain versus residual CNNs, very deep plain tanh training, and Fixup residual training without normalization.
Effects of activation-matched initialization, orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization, and initialization-dependent trainable depth.
Recovery above the initial stability threshold, curvature reduction, edge-of-stability dynamics, and divergence below the threshold.
Batch normalization's effect on accuracy gain per training step and learning-rate tolerance, and normalization-free residual training using Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: There are no extracted rows to fix. The omitted findings concern different interventions or outcomes and are already broadly declared in rows_left_out; they do not justify version-specific verdicts.

versions.untested_parts: Whether sufficiently large convolutional networks reach zero or near-zero training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, including corrupted or random labels; effects of model size, stopping, and regularization.
Teacher-student two-layer ReLU spurious minima and the effect of student width.
Plain versus residual network depth, special initialization for deep plain tanh networks, and normalization-free residual training.
Activation-matched initialization, orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization, and trainability at extreme depth.
Training above the stability threshold, edge-of-stability dynamics, and divergence below the threshold.

The paper discusses LayerNorm-related effects, not batch normalization’s effect on training speed or learning-rate tolerance. Its benchmark comparisons concern NaP and do not isolate or report the V6 batch-normalization outcomes.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
